To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the anthropogenic contribution to global and local mean relative sea level rise since 1900 is virtually certain (i.e., at least 45%), and that the anthropogenic component of local relative sea level rise is overestimated when the atmospheric contribution is not accounted for.

(1) natural variability in the rate of sea-level rise is underestimated in many records; (2) the anthropogenic contribution to the observed sea-level rise is larger than previously assumed; and (3) the anthropogenic component is likely to continue increasing in the near future.

the upper range for the contribution of anthropogenic sea-level rise is at least 45%, and that this estimate is robust with respect to the choice of the model, the observational data set, the time period and the statistical approach.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the detection of long-term trends in sea level rise, which is a major challenge in the context of the ongoing climate change.
the detection of anthropogenic foot-prints in sea-level records.
the detection and attribution of sea level changes.

anthropogenic contributions to LMSL have been underestimated in the past, while the GMSL has been estimated correctly.

the anthropogenic signal is not only detectable, but also dominant.
